newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Speculation danger seen for HK mass housing market.
newsitem.headline: Speculation danger seen for HK mass housing market.

text.p: Rampant speculation in Hong Kong's luxury property market could spill over into the lower cost mass housing market, property consultancy Brooke Hillier Parker warned on Tuesday.

Increasing prices in the residential property market was a serious concern, particularly in the mass market of flats worth HK$10 million and below category, Nicholas Brooke, senior partner of the consultancy, told a news conference.
"There (in the mass market) I think the greed factor is becoming more and more prominent -- when I mentioned the greed factor, I was talking about speculation," he said.
"That, I think, is something that we can't ignore and is something that happened at the top end (and) is now moving down to the (mass) market," Brooke said.
Prices in the luxury residential market rose about 35 percent in 1996, while average growth of 24 percent was recorded in the mass housing market, recent research by Brooke Hillier Parker showed.
Strong upward pressure would continue, especially in the first part of the year, Brooke warned.
"It's Chinese New Year time (in February) and that's bonus time for a lot of people, I think that's going to fuel the fire," he said.
Brooke expected a strong rise in housing prices in 1997 unless effective measures were taken to curb speculation.
"I think we could see 20-30 percent in the mass market which is very unhealthy in my view and not acceptable," he said.
Brooke said he would like to see residential property prices kept within a more reasonable growth rate of about 10-15 percent a year.
The consultancy also said property developers and banks should help to curb the possible price spiral, which if left unchecked could lead to government intervention.
Brooke noted a number of developers have agreed they would limit the number of companies, as opposed to individuals, that can bid for new flats.
"I would like to see this become a standard that no company can purchase a new property of between zero and HK$10 million and developers would only accept offers from individuals," he added.

Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd has sought to help cool speculation by restricting the number of potential home buyers registered as limited companies to a maximum of 20 for every 100 registered buyers in its East Point City development.
Brooke also suggested banks look at cutting back the ceiling on mortages provided to flat buyers to 60 perent of a flat's value from the current 70 percent.
"It's painful and it will hurt the first-time buyers, but in the long term I think it would take some of the heat out of the situation," he added.

Brooke said government intervention, while not a strong option, was further avoidable if the industry took initiative to curb speculative price rises, but he also said he would like to see speculators taxed.
"The government has identified a number of traders, people who are speculating in the market, and I think they should be seen to be taxed," he said.
Many of Hong Kong's legislators and citizens have complained that residential prices had gone skyward and out of the affordibility of salaried people.
